summary: Defines a portion of the MIB for monitoring and controlling network devices with APPN, IBM's Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking, capabilities. It replaces RFC 2155. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: These are dials and switches for watching and steering a special kind of older IBM network, so managers can see what is going on.

questions: how to manage appn devices with snmp
what is a branch network node
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and steering IBM APPN nodes, ports, link stations, topology and sessions.

tldr.problem: Devices that run APPN, the peer-to-peer part of IBM's Systems Network Architecture, had no standard way to be monitored or controlled with the Internet's SNMP management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module, APPN-MIB, with groups of objects for the node, the network topology, the local topology, the directory, classes of service and intermediate sessions, plus one alert trap.
tldr.outcome: A management station can read configuration and status and can activate or deactivate ports and link stations. The module deliberately excludes node configuration, endpoint sessions, DLUR and HPR management. It obsoletes RFC 2155.

today: RFC 2455 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it. It obsoletes RFC 2155.

sections.title: What the APPN MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2455 is a product of the SNA NAU Services MIB Working Group. It defines a MIB module for managing devices with APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) capabilities. APPN is the part of IBM's Systems Network Architecture (SNA) that supports peer-to-peer networking, carrying both independent and dependent LU session traffic.

The module is written in SMIv2, one part of the SNMP management framework that the RFC summarizes: an architecture, a way to describe and name managed objects, message protocols, protocol operations, and a set of applications with access control. A version for SMIv1 can be produced by translation, and the RFC notes that objects needing Counter64 cannot be translated.

The RFC points to other MIBs for neighbouring topics: the SNA NAU and APPC MIBs for sessions, RFC 2232 for DLUR and RFC 2238 for HPR.
sections.eli5: An old kind of computer network had no standard control panel. This document designs one, so the same tools used for other networks can read the gauges on this one.

sections.title: The APPN Nodes the MIB Describes
sections.content:
An APPN network is made of nodes joined by transmission groups (TGs). The MIB has to cover several node types.

  • Network nodes (NNs) provide directory and routing functions for session establishment, and can be session end points or intermediate nodes.
  • End nodes (ENs) are session end points that get directory and routing help from network nodes over CP-CP sessions.
  • LEN nodes are also end points but do not support CP-CP sessions, so they need manual definitions.
  • Border nodes join networks for session establishment without fully merging them.
  • Branch network nodes (BrNNs) are like border nodes with minimal functions, and look like an end node to upstream network nodes. A BrNN reports endNode in appnNodeType and identifies itself as a BrNN through appnNodeBrNn.
  • Virtual routing nodes (VRNs) are not real nodes but shared definitions on a transport such as a LAN, letting real nodes link up without defining each other's link-level addresses.

Ports and link stations are the node's interface to the data link control layer. A link station uses a port to connect to another node, and that connection establishes a TG.
sections.eli5: Think of a town with big post offices, small mailboxes and a few shortcut roads. The MIB has a way to describe each kind of building and each road between them.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The module groups its objects under appnObjects, with a separate appnTraps branch. The six object groups are:

  • appnNode: node-wide information for every node type, including general information, network-node and end-node specifics, the port table, the link station tables and the VRN table.
  • appnNn: the network topology database kept in network nodes, covering network nodes, VRNs and the TGs between them.
  • appnLocalTopology: the local topology database kept in all nodes, including the node's own TGs.
  • appnDir: LU location information from the directory database.
  • appnCos: class of service information, including mode-to-COS mapping, transmission priority, and node and TG weights.
  • appnSessIntermediate: intermediate sessions passing through the node, including those carried over RTP connections by HPR.

Topology tables are first indexed by the flow reduction sequence number (FRSN) used in topology exchanges between network nodes. A management station can therefore fetch only incremental updates, since the agent updates the FRSN of new or changed resources. To draw a full picture of the network, an application can query the topology tables of a single network node, then follow branch TGs and local TG tables to find BrNNs, end nodes and LEN nodes.
sections.eli5: The control panel is split into drawers: one for the machine itself, one for the map of the whole network, one for its own roads, one for the phone book, one for road-use rules and one for the conversations passing through.

sections.title: How SNA Names Are Handled
sections.content:
SNA names such as LU, CP, COS and mode names may be padded with blanks in SNA formats, and those blanks are not significant. In this MIB the agent leaves them out. For example, the COS name #INTER is returned with length 6 and no padding, however it appeared in the BIND request unit. The one exception is the all-blank mode name, which is returned as 8 blank spaces.

When a name is used as a table index, trailing blanks are significant, so an index of #INTER does not match the row indexed #INTER. Since the agent never has padded indices, the only reason for a management station to add blanks is to start GetNext processing at a chosen point, for example M to start at the first row beginning with M or a later letter.
sections.eli5: Some old names came with extra empty spaces on the end, like a name tag with spare room. The MIB trims the spare room when it reports a name, but when you look something up by name the spaces count.

sections.title: Monitoring and Controlling
sections.content:
The listed management functions are: activating and deactivating ports and link stations; monitoring configuration parameters for the node, ports, link stations, VRNs and classes of service; monitoring operational parameters for ports, link stations, VRNs, topology, directory and intermediate sessions; history of link station errors during connection establishment or that ended a connection; deactivating intermediate sessions; and traps for SNA Management Services (SNA/MS) alert conditions.

Control works through read-write objects. appnPortCommand lets a management station activate, deactivate or recycle a port (recycle means deactivate and then immediately activate). The value ready is returned on a GET until a SET has been processed. The link station table has a matching appnLsCommand. Port state is reported in appnPortOperState as inactive, pending active, active or pending inactive.

The appnLsStatusTable records errors with connections to adjacent nodes, including sense data captured at connection failures. How many entries are kept is a product option.

One trap is defined, alertTrap. It carries a 32-bit SNA/MS Alert ID number and, where possible, the affected object, and implementing it is optional for a product.
sections.eli5: You can look at a gauge to see if a door is open or closed, and you can press a button to open it, close it, or close it and instantly open it again. If something goes wrong, a bell rings and says which gauge to check.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2155
sections.content:
RFC 2455 obsoletes RFC 2155, with changes for additions to the APPN architecture and some implementation experience. The listed changes:

  • New objects for multi-link TGs: appnLsMltgMember, appnNnTgFRMltgLinkType, appnLocalTgMltgLinkType and appnLocalEnTgMltgLinkType.
  • New objects and clarified values for branch network nodes: appnNodeBrNn, appnNnNodeFRBranchAwareness, appnNnTgFRBranchTg and appnLocalTgBranchLinkType.
  • A new object, appnNodeLsCounterType, that tells which type of ANR traffic is returned in the link station traffic counters.
  • The appnNodeMibVersion object is deprecated.
  • Miscellaneous editorial changes.
sections.eli5: This is the second version of the control panel, with new switches for two new kinds of network buildings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some management information can be sensitive, so authentication of SNMP requests and controlled access SHOULD be used in such environments. The RFC points to the user-based security model for authentication and the view-based access control model for access control.

Five read-only objects (appnNnTgFRSecurity, appnLocalTgSecurity, appnLocalEnTgSecurity, appnCosTgRowSecurityMin and appnCosTgRowSecurityMax) show the potential path of secure data, and could reveal a security exposure caused by a misconfigured agent. Nothing else read-only reports passwords or user data, but some enterprises treat their network configuration and usage data as corporate assets and may want to restrict access.

Four read-write objects can affect network operations, and SNMP access to them should be restricted: appnNodeNnSafeStoreFreq (0 or a very large value effectively turns off safe storing of topology data), appnPortCommand and appnLsCommand (which can activate, deactivate or recycle, disrupting users), and appnIsInSessState (setting it to inactive ends an active SNA session).
sections.eli5: Some gauges are fine for anyone to read, but a few buttons can shut things down. Only trusted people should be allowed to press those.
